newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Cable vols rise, bias to sterling puts.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Cable vols rise, bias to sterling puts.

text.p: Implied volatilities for short-dated dollar/Sterling options raced higher Tuesday as the pound staged an unexpected reversal of fortune.
At the same time, implied volatilities for one-month dollar/mark and dollar/yen options climbed, driven largely by cross activity between the mark, pound and yen.

"Sterling crosses are moving down; that's creating one source of volatility. And the yen is moving up on a cross basis so that's creating volatility," said Oliver Jefferson, vice president at Societe General.
The net effect was to increase volatility on dollar/pair options, and to alter several dollar/pair risk reversals, dealers said.

After showing a firm bias for Sterling calls in the London session, the one-month 25 delta dollar/sterling risk reversal flipped to show a slight skew toward Sterling puts by midday in New York, dealers said.
Over the same period, the dollar/yen risk reversal, which had been flirting with a slight preference for yen puts, swung back to show a more familiar bias toward yen calls.
At noon CST/1800 GMT, implied volatility for one-month dollar/Sterling was up half a percentage point from the start of the U.S. session at 7.75 percent, OTC dealers said.

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark at-the-money options was 8.35 percent, up 1.5 percent from Monday's U.S. open but unchanged on the day. The rise in volatility occurred during Monday's U.S. session and overnight in Europe as the mark fell to a 23-month low against the U.S. currency.
"Dollar/mark has not advanced during the New York session whereas sterling has collapsed during the U.S. session. That's probably the most significant difference," Jefferson said.

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen options was also higher, at 7.1/7.3 percent versus 6.6/6.9 percent early in the session, as yen staged a convincing rally against marks, Swiss francs and Sterling and, through those currencies, the dollar, dealers said.

One dealer, with a Canadian bank, said dollar/yen volatility was also higher as a result of a large strangle -- rumored to be worth more than one billion dollars -- which traded during the European session.
It was said to be a four month option with strikes at 104 yen and 112.50 yen, the dealer said.
Implied volatilities were also higher at Chicago Mercantile Exchange's IMM, where currency futures options traders were unusually busy.
"The pound's screaming, the yen's screaming," said one IMM dealer of implied volatilities. "Everything's going through the roof."
